title: Does splaying every BST preorder take linear total time?
formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that, for every n and every two binary search trees A and B on the same n distinct ordered keys, searching for the keys of preorder(B), in order, using bottom-up splaying starting from A costs at most Cn? Define preorder recursively as root, then left-subtree preorder, then right-subtree preorder. Every key is searched once. Charge one unit per visited search-path node and one per single rotation; perform no insertions or deletions.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal linear bound for all pairs (A,B), or show that the ratio of this cost to n is unbounded over a family of such pairs. A bound requiring the traversal tree B to be balanced does not settle the proposition.
definitions: A binary search tree stores one key per node, all left descendants smaller and all right descendants larger. On a search for x, first follow comparisons from the root to x. Then repeatedly splay x: if its parent is the root, rotate x over its parent (zig); if x and its parent are both left children or both right children, rotate the parent over the grandparent and then x over the parent (zig-zig); otherwise rotate x over its parent and then over its former grandparent (zig-zag). The same node x remains the splayed node until it becomes root. The arbitrary starting tree A and the tree B defining the permutation are separate inputs to the mathematical claim; splay receives only the search requests.
context:
This asks about a particularly structured access sequence, rather than every possible sequence in the dynamic-optimality conjecture. A traversal visits each key exactly once, but its order reflects a second tree that may be quite different from the tree currently being searched. The proposed linear total bound says that this hidden structure is enough for splaying to adapt efficiently.

For example, the preorder of a balanced tree on seven keys can be 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7. This is not a sorted scan: after finishing one subtree, the sequence can jump to a distant part of the key order. If the starting tree is a long chain, even the first requested key can be far from the root. The question concerns the total cost, so a single expensive access is harmless if later savings pay for it.

The distinction between access and insertion matters. Building a tree by inserting the preorder keys into an empty splay tree is a different operation sequence, and that version is known to be linear. Linear access bounds are also known when the tree defining the preorder is weight-balanced. Neither restriction covers all traversal trees.

This is a useful intermediate target because the input family is precise and recognizable. A proof can exploit the recursive order of the permutation; a counterexample would have to show that this order still permits repeated expensive restructuring.
why: I include this as a concrete test of whether a local restructuring rule detects global order in requests without being told that order. It isolates a major obstacle in understanding adaptive search trees while avoiding the full freedom of arbitrary repeated-access sequences.

progress.text: The traversal conjecture originates in the introduction of splay trees, as recorded in the later primary studies.
Levy and Tarjan prove linear-time preorder and postorder insertion into an empty tree, and linear access when the traversal tree is weight-balanced.
The new splay competitive analysis still records traversal optimality only in special settings. Its competitive factor is not constant.
